title: A Plague Beyond Memory
sum: Joel opens with a disaster so large that the elders are asked whether anything like it has ever happened, and told to pass the story to their grandchildren. Locusts, four kinds of them in a row, have stripped the land of grain, new wine and oil. Joel then calls everyone in turn to mourn: the drunkards who have lost their wine, the farmers and vinedressers who have lost the harvest, and above all the priests, because the daily grain and drink offerings have stopped in the house of the LORD.

The chapter ends in prayer. "Alas for the day!" Joel says, for the day of the LORD is close, and it comes "like havoc from the Almighty". The last verses turn from the people to the LORD: fire has eaten the pastures, the streams are dry, and even the animals of the field gasp for him. The plague is not treated as an accident. It is the nation's cue to fast, to gather and to cry out.
readings: Locust swarms hit Palestine and Syria in 1915, and in many other years, and observers describe the same things Joel names: land stripped bare, a darkened sky, fields and trees eaten, a famine that ends the sacrifices. On this reading chapter 1 is an eyewitness poem, and 'the day of the LORD' is Joel's name for what he is living through.
Read as an army told as a swarm

The locusts are called a 'nation' with teeth like a lion's (1:6), and the plague is the LORD's own judgment. Some ancient and medieval readers saw an invading army behind the locusts from the first chapter, and the four names as four empires.

The chapter is built as a call to mourn, addressed to each group in turn (elders, drunkards, farmers, priests), and ending in the prayer of one voice. It may have been composed for a public fast and used in the Temple liturgy for such days.

views.H: A swarm of locusts followed by drought and fire struck Judah in a year the book does not name. The Temple stands, the priests serve in it, and the elders lead the people. There is no king and no foreign army. The date is debated: before 586 BC (a ninth-century setting in the reign of the boy-king Joash, or the eighth century), or after the return from exile (fifth or fourth century). See the book's opening pages.
views.C: Verses 2-4 open the book like a prophet's lecture to elders; 5-14 are summonses to mourn ('wake up', 'wail', 'be ashamed', 'tie on sackcloth', 'consecrate a fast'); 15-20 are an alarm and a prayer. The four locust names stand together nowhere else in the Bible. The phrase 'the day of the LORD is close' (1:15) is shared with Isaiah 13:6 and Ezekiel 30:3, and some scholars see Joel using the earlier prophets as a source (Bergler), or as a model for a new literary 'day of the LORD' tradition. The play on 'dry' and 'ashamed' (1:10-12) is a pun in the Hebrew that English cannot carry.
views.J: Rashi says the four words of 1:4 are species of locust, and Radak says the four kinds came one after another over four years (see the note at 1:4). The Mishnah (Taanit 3:5) lists the locust ('arbeh) and the stripping locust (chasil), two of Joel's four words, among the troubles for which the community cries out, and Joel 1:14 and 2:15-16 are the model texts for a public fast with an assembly. This edition did not check what the Targum says on this chapter.
views.X: Jerome, in his Commentary on Joel, reports a reading of the four locusts as four successive empires and sets his own alongside it. Cyril of Alexandria, Theodoret and Calvin (in his lectures on the Twelve) also wrote on Joel; this edition did not check what they say on this chapter. The chapter's Lenten use begins with Joel 2:12, but chapter 1's call to the priests to put on sackcloth and spend the night in prayer is also a pattern for church fasts.
views.F: Some interpreters (and Revelation 9:1-11, which draws on Joel) see the locusts as a picture of end-time judgment. Dispensational teachers distinguish the plague of Joel's day from a future 'locust army'; amillennial readers see the plague and its day as a type that every generation meets in its own way.

deep.h: A year without harvest, step by step
deep.b:
Joel's list of losses follows the farmer's year. The grain is lost first (1:10), then the new wine and fresh oil, the other two of the three gifts of the land (Deuteronomy 7:13; 11:14). Then the fruit trees go: vine, fig, pomegranate, palm and apple (1:12). Then the stored grain: the storehouses are bare and the granaries fall down for lack of use (1:17). Last come the animals: the cattle wander for lack of grass and the sheep suffer (1:18). Each loss touches worship, because grain, wine and oil were what the priests offered every day (1:9, 13).

The effect on the reader is to see the plague as damage to the whole order of life under the covenant, which the law had said would happen if Israel broke faith (Deuteronomy 28:38-42), though Joel never says why it happened. He gives no sin to confess in chapter 1. That silence is itself a question the book answers differently from Amos 4:9, which says the LORD sent locusts and still the people did not turn back.

Joel plays on sound. Hovish can mean "it is dry" or "it is put to shame", and the book uses both (1:10-12, 17), so the same word describes withered crops and humiliated farmers. Shod and Shaddai ("havoc" and "the Almighty", 1:15) share their opening sounds. Yeleq, chasil, gazam, 'arbeh have no English counterparts and the Plain keeps four English words so the reader can see four names. The notes mark where a pun is lost.

echoes: Exodus 10:1-15; Deuteronomy 28:38-42; 1 Kings 8:37; Psalm 78:46; Isaiah 13:6; Ezekiel 30:2-3; Obadiah 15; Amos 4:9; Zephaniah 1:7, 14; Revelation 9:1-11

settings.what: Joel's call to the elders and the four locusts
settings.by: Joel, son of Pethuel, as the prophet of the LORD
settings.to: The elders and everyone who lives in the land of Judah, the whole community at a time of crisis
settings.when: After a locust plague and drought have stripped the land, in a year the book does not date
settings.why: To make the nation listen to something so large it needs a hearing: a disaster without a parallel in anyone's memory, to be told to the children and grandchildren like the plagues of Egypt. Knowing the audience shows that the first call is to those with the memory and the authority, the elders, and not to the king or the army.
settings.readers: For later readers of the Twelve, the story became part of the book's setting for the day of the LORD.
views: A speech in the days of King Joash or later in the eighth century, to a Judah with elders and priests and a Temple, and perhaps a king not named.
A speech to the Persian-period community of Judah, led by elders and priests, with no king, as the Temple community in Ezra and Nehemiah was.

settings.what: A call to mourn for the drunkards, farmers and vinedressers
settings.to: Drinkers of wine, farmers and vinedressers (the people who lose first), and the personified land
settings.when: As the harvest fails and the wine is cut off
settings.why: To make the loss personal and concrete: wine no longer reaches the mouth, wheat and barley are lost, the vine and fig fail and joy dries up. The list starts with people who would not normally be at the center of a call to repentance, so that every kind of person sees himself in it.
settings.readers: Later readers could see the land itself mourn, as in Jeremiah 12:4 and Hosea 4:3.

settings.what: The call to the priests and the fast
settings.to: The priests, the ministers of the altar, and through them the elders and all who live in the land
settings.when: When the daily grain and drink offerings have stopped for lack of grain and wine
settings.why: To turn the nation's loss into worship. Priests are told to wear sackcloth and keep a night vigil, and the elders and people are summoned to the house of the LORD for a fast and a sacred assembly. The priests are told because they alone can lead the community's cry, and because the loss is theirs too.
settings.readers: For the Temple community, the pattern of priests, elders and people gathered at the Temple was the model for every fast after it.
views: A fast of the whole community, called by the elders, as in 1 Kings 21:9 and 2 Chronicles 20:3.
Some think the text was shaped for use at the Temple in times of drought, as Mishnah Taanit later describes.

settings.by: Joel, first to the people, then as one voice crying to the LORD
settings.to: The people, and then the LORD himself
settings.when: As the drought and fire follow the locusts
settings.why: To tell the people that this is not an end but a sign of something larger, the day of the LORD, and to model the prayer that follows. The prophet prays first, and even the animals join him. Knowing this, the chapter is a pattern: the prophet does what he asks the people to do.
settings.readers: For readers of the Twelve, 'the day of the LORD is close' joins Joel to Obadiah, Zephaniah and Amos.

title: Even Now, Turn Back
sum: The chapter opens with an alarm. A horn is blown in Zion, and an army that looks like horses and moves like locusts climbs walls and enters houses like a thief; before it the earth shakes and the stars go dark, and the LORD himself leads it. Then comes the turn. "Even now," the LORD says, "turn back to me with your whole heart." Tear your hearts, not your clothes, for he is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, great in loyal love, and he changes his mind about the harm. The whole community, from the elders to the nursing babies and the bridegroom, is called to the Temple, and the priests pray.

The LORD answers. He is jealous for his land, and he promises grain, new wine and oil, drives out the northern one, tells the soil and animals to stop fearing, gives the rains and gives back the years the locusts ate. After this, the LORD says, he will pour out his Spirit on all flesh: sons and daughters, old and young, even the slaves. There will be signs in the sky, and everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be rescued. These verses (2:28-32) are the passage Peter quotes at Pentecost (Acts 2:17-21).
readings: Read as a plague and its end
The invasion of 2:1-11 is the locusts of chapter 1 seen again, now coming in a wave. The fast of 2:12-17 ends the plague, and 2:18-27 reports the harvest and the rains that follow.
The army of 2:1-11 is an invasion from the north (2:20) by a human power: Assyria, Babylon, or Gog and the nations in a later age. The locusts are an image of it.
Read as the day of the LORD in stages

The chapter moves through three parts of one day: the alarm and the army (2:1-11), the offer of rescue (2:12-17) and the answer (2:18-32). The army, the repentance and the Spirit are three scenes in the one book of the day.

views.H: The setting is Judah's fast at the Temple, led by priests and elders. Verse 2:20 names an enemy, 'the northern one', whose identity is debated; 2:25 says the plague lasted years and was the LORD's army. If Joel is early the setting is Judah under a regent-priest; if late, the Persian-period Temple community. The Spirit promise (2:28-29) has no historical fulfillment recorded in the Hebrew Bible; the New Testament sees it at Pentecost.
views.C: Is 2:1-11 the same locusts as chapter 1 or a different, human, enemy? Does 2:18 begin a report of the LORD's answer or a promise? Do 2:28-32 (Hebrew 3:1-5) belong with chapter 2 or with the 'day of the LORD' judgment of chapter 3? The word 'afterward' joins them, and most commentators see Joel 2:28-3:21 as one future-oriented section. The creed of 2:13 is a quotation of Exodus 34:6-7 with one new ending (see the note). The 'teacher of righteousness' reading of 2:23 has been tied to Qumran but without evidence.
views.J: Joel 2:13 is the best-known verse of Joel in Jewish tradition: the Mishnah (Taanit 2:1) quotes it on fast days for rain, in the elder's admonition. Joel 2:12-17 supplies the model of the community fast. The Talmud (Sukkah 52a) reads hatsefoni, "the northern one" of 2:20, as tsafun, "hidden": the evil inclination, which hides in a person's heart, one of the seven names the baraita gives it. Rashi also gives the locust and Assyria as readings of the northern one, and Ibn Ezra and Radak take it as the locust (see the note at 2:20). Rashi reads the "teacher" of 2:23 as the prophets who teach Israel to turn back. Numbers Rabbah (15:25) quotes Joel 2:28 for the saying that in this world individuals prophesied, but in the world to come all Israel will be prophets.
views.X: The church reads 2:12-17 as the call of Lent and Ash Wednesday, and 2:28-32 as fulfilled at Pentecost (Acts 2:17-21), with Romans 10:13 taking 2:32 as a promise for all who call on the Lord Jesus. Calvin's commentary on Acts takes Peter's words as a claim of fulfillment; Jerome's commentary follows the Vulgate's 'teacher of righteousness' (2:23) and applies it to Christ; Pentecostal and charismatic Christians read the passage as the promise of the Spirit for every believer. See the cards. This edition did not check Ephrem, Cyril of Alexandria, Theodoret, Chrysostom, Luther or Pusey on this chapter.
views.F: Many dispensational teachers hold that Peter at Pentecost used Joel as an illustration or a first installment, with the full fulfillment (the Spirit on Israel, the cosmic signs of 2:30-31) still to come at the end of the age. Amillennial readers hold that the 'last days' began at Pentecost and run until Christ returns, so the signs of 2:30-31 belong to the end of that period. Jewish messianic readings expect the Spirit in the messianic age.

deep.h: Joel's creed: what Joel changes in Exodus 34
deep.b:
When the LORD showed himself to Moses after the golden calf, he named himself: "The LORD, the LORD, a God compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, great in loyal love and faithfulness, keeping loyal love to thousands, forgiving guilt, rebellion and sin" (Exodus 34:6-7). That creed becomes the Bible's central description of God (Numbers 14:18; Nehemiah 9:17; Psalm 86:15; 103:8; 145:8). Joel 2:13 and Jonah 4:2 use it in nearly the same form, with the same new ending: "and he changes his mind about the harm."

Joel leaves out "faithfulness", "forgiving guilt, rebellion and sin" and the warning that the guilty are not cleared. He adds the line about changing his mind. In Joel the creed does not answer the question "what does God do with sin?" It answers a narrower one, "may we hope that this disaster will be lifted?" and the answer is a conditional yes: "Who knows?" (2:14).

deep.h: Acts 2 and Joel 2: how Peter's quotation works
deep.b:
Peter says that the outpouring on the day of Pentecost is "the very thing spoken through Joel the prophet" (Acts 2:16). He quotes Joel 2:28-32 in the form of the Greek Bible, with the differences listed in the note on 2:28. Readers differ on what "this is that" means. Some say it is a claim of fulfillment: the Spirit of the last days has come. Some say it is a claim of the same kind of event, an outpouring that begins the last days, with part of Joel's picture (the sun and moon) still to come. Some say Peter takes Joel as a pattern, not a prediction. The Hebrew of Joel says nothing about tongues or a house, and speaks of prophecy, dreams and visions.

The Greek reading "after these things" became "in the last days" on Peter's lips, which makes the claim explicit: the age of the Spirit is the age of the last days (compare Acts 2:33, 38-39).

deep.title: Claude's theory: the slave verse is the hinge of the book
deep.b: My own reading, not a standard one. Joel begins by calling the elders, then drunkards, farmers, vinedressers and priests, one group after another, as if reading a register of the community. At the book's middle (2:16) he calls the elders, children, bridegroom and bride, a register of the whole community again. In the Spirit promise (2:28-29) the register runs the other way: sons and daughters, old and young, then slaves. The rank order of society is read three times, in mourning, in assembly and in the gift of the Spirit. The gift reaches to the bottom, and that is the surprise of 2:29. I know of no commentary that sets out the three registers this way, so treat the pattern as a suggestion.

echoes: Exodus 34:6-7; Numbers 14:18; Numbers 11:29; 2 Samuel 12:22; Nehemiah 9:17; Psalm 79:10; Psalm 103:8; Psalm 145:8; Isaiah 13:10; Isaiah 44:3; Ezekiel 32:7; Ezekiel 39:29; Jonah 3:9; Jonah 4:2; Zephaniah 2:3; Malachi 3:2; Matthew 24:29; Acts 2:16-21; Romans 10:13; Revelation 6:12; Revelation 9:7-9

settings.what: The alarm and the army of the day of the LORD
settings.to: The people of Zion and all who live in the land, summoned by a horn in the city
settings.when: As the plague deepens or after it, with the day of the LORD seen as coming
settings.why: To shake the nation awake. The horn is the alarm for war, and what comes is described as an irresistible army that is, in the end, the LORD's own. Knowing this, the terror of the picture is not an end in itself: it prepares the listener for the turn at 2:12.
settings.readers: For readers across the centuries the passage became the book's 'day of the LORD' picture, used by Revelation 9 for its locusts.
views: A swarm told as an army.
A human invasion, drawn with locust images.
The enemy of the last days, as in Ezekiel 38-39.

settings.what: The LORD's call to turn back, and the priests' prayer
settings.by: The LORD (2:12), then Joel (2:13-17), including a prayer for the priests to say
settings.to: The whole community: elders, people, children, nursing babies, bridegroom and bride, and the priests who stand between the porch and the altar
settings.when: On the day of the fast and sacred assembly at the Temple
settings.why: To turn the nation from fear to repentance, with a reason: the LORD's own nature. The priests are given the words to say, which shows that the prophet is writing a liturgy for the Temple. They appeal to his people, his inheritance and his name before the nations. The call 'even now' means that the disaster is not too late to turn.
settings.readers: The Temple community, and then every community of Israel on a fast day, used the passage to teach that outward signs without inward turning are not enough.
views: Joel records a real fast and its prayer.
The prayer is a model text for Temple fast days, set down by the prophet.

settings.what: The LORD's answer: the land restored
settings.by: Joel, reporting the LORD's answer; the LORD speaks in the first person from 2:19
settings.to: The people who fasted, and, in turn, the land, the animals and the people of Zion
settings.when: After the fast, or as a promise made for the day the community turns
settings.why: To announce the end of the plague and the shame. The LORD removes the northern one, gives back the harvest and the rains, and promises that he is in their midst and that they will never again be ashamed. Knowing the audience shows what this does: it is the answer to the priests' question 'Where is their God?'
settings.readers: For later readers it became the model of what repentance can bring, and the passage 'I will give you back the years' was applied to many later disasters.
views: The verbs of 2:18 tell what happened after the fast.
2:18 begins a future promise to a community that has just repented.

settings.what: The outpouring of the Spirit and the day of the LORD
settings.to: The people of Zion and Jerusalem, 'your sons and daughters, your old men and young men', and the slaves
settings.when: 'After this', a time not dated; in the Hebrew Bible it is the start of a new chapter
settings.why: To widen the promise. Beyond the end of the plague there is a gift of the Spirit that belongs to the whole community, not to a few leaders, and a day of the LORD that comes with signs and a rescue for all who call on him. The words answer Moses's wish that all the LORD's people were prophets (Numbers 11:29). Knowing the first hearers shows whom the promise was first made to, and the views below differ on whether that was Israel alone or all peoples.
settings.readers: For the first Christians (Acts 2) the promise was for all who are far off, from Jews to Gentiles.
views: The promise was first to Judah and Jerusalem and the nation.
'All flesh' means every human being, including the nations, as in Acts 2:39.

traditions.q: Is the outpouring of the Spirit in Joel 2:28-32 a once-for-all event at Pentecost or a pattern for the whole church age?
views: Pentecost is the one great outpouring on the Church, in which the Spirit was given to the apostles and, through them, to all. The same Spirit is given to each believer in baptism and, in fullness, in the sacrament of Confirmation, which the Catechism links to the outpouring on the apostles at Pentecost (Catechism 731, 1302).

Pentecost is the birthday of the Church, when the Spirit came on the apostles. The Spirit is given to each person at baptism and chrismation (anointing with oil, done right after baptism), the seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit. In the Byzantine rite, the Pentecost Vespers includes the reading of Joel 2:23-3:5 (the Greek numbering, English 2:23-32) among its Old Testament readings.

The Holy Spirit is given through the Word and the sacraments (Augsburg Confession V); Pentecost is the first giving of that Spirit to the Church. Luther rejects any claim to a Spirit apart from the Word, and teaches that the Spirit calls, gathers and enlightens the church by the gospel.

The 'last days' began with Christ and Pentecost and continue until his return; the Spirit is given to all believers, as Calvin reads Acts 2:16-17. Many Reformed teachers hold that the miraculous signs of Pentecost belong to the apostolic age (a cessationist view, resting on the Westminster Confession 1.1), while others, in the Reformed charismatic tradition, hold that the gifts continue.

Baptists hold that the Holy Spirit is given to every believer and gives gifts for service in the church (Baptist Faith and Message, 2000, article II). Pentecost is the Spirit's coming on the church. Baptist churches are divided on whether miraculous gifts such as tongues continue, and the confession does not settle it.

Joel's promise is for every believer, and Pentecost is repeated in the 'baptism in the Holy Spirit', an experience after conversion, evidenced by speaking in tongues, that empowers witness. Joel 2:23 and 2:28 are often taken as 'the early and latter rain' of a last revival.

Many dispensational teachers hold that Joel's prophecy is addressed to Israel and will be completely fulfilled in the age of the kingdom; at Pentecost Peter showed what the promised Spirit is like. Progressive dispensationalists (such as Darrell Bock) hold that the Spirit's coming was a first fulfillment, with the rest to come.

traditions.q: Should the church keep fast days like Joel's, and when?
views: Fasting is one of the three forms of penance, with prayer and almsgiving (Catechism 1434). Ash Wednesday, the first day of Lent, opens with Joel 2:12-18; Ash Wednesday and Good Friday are days of fasting and abstinence for Catholics aged 18 to 59 (Code of Canon Law 1251-1252).
Great Lent, the Wednesdays and Fridays of the year and other seasons are times of fasting, which is joined to repentance, prayer and care for the poor. The fast is of foods and also of the passions.

Fasting and bodily preparation are a good outward discipline, but not a work that earns anything, and no day is required by God's law (Augsburg Confession XXVI; Luther's Small Catechism, on the Sacrament of the Altar).

Calvin teaches that fasting is a lawful help in prayer and repentance, and that public fasts should be called by the church in times of need, with Joel 2:15-16 as a model (Institutes 4.12). Fast days are a matter of Christian freedom, not an obligation of days or foods. The Westminster Directory for Public Worship sets out rules for solemn fasts.

The 1662 Book of Common Prayer lists the days of fasting and abstinence (Lent, the Ember days and Fridays) and its Ash Wednesday service, the Commination, has Joel 2:12-17 as its Epistle; the common lectionary also gives Joel 2:1-2, 12-17 for Ash Wednesday. Practice differs between provinces.

Baptist churches have no set fast days (the Baptist Faith and Message sets none); fasting is left to the believer and the congregation (Matthew 6:16-18), and many call a day of prayer and fasting in time of need as Joel does.

traditions.q: Does God really change his mind (Joel 2:13-14)?
views: God does not change, and Scripture speaks of his repenting by accommodation to our understanding, as a human father might (Calvin, Institutes 1.17.12-13; Westminster Confession 2.1). What changes is the outcome as we see it; God's decree does not.

God is unchanging, and the change in the effects of his action is real in us and not in him (Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I q.19 a.7); the Catechism teaches that God is faithful and does not abandon his word (Catechism 212). The language of relenting expresses the change in how God deals with a repentant people.

Lutheran teachers read the language of God's regret as God speaking in human terms, and hold that God himself does not change; Luther takes this line in his Lectures on Genesis on the passages where God is said to be sorry.

God is unchanging in his essence and truly relates to his creatures in his energies. Warnings of judgment are conditional and are meant to turn the sinner, so that God does not carry out a threat when a person repents; his love is the same throughout.
God's threats of harm are conditional on the people's response, and his character does not change, but his dealing with each person changes as the person answers (a view found in Wesleyan teaching).

Some Evangelical teachers, the open theists (for example Clark Pinnock and John Sanders), hold that God really responds to human choices and that the passages about relenting should be read as they stand, not softened. Most Evangelicals do not follow them and hold that God's knowledge and purposes do not change.

title: The Valley of Decision
sum: The last chapter looks ahead. The LORD will turn the fortunes of Judah and Jerusalem around, gather all the nations in the Valley of Jehoshaphat, and put them on trial for what they did to his people: scattering them, dividing the land, selling boys and girls for a prostitute and a drink. Tyre, Sidon and Philistia are singled out for selling Judeans to the Greeks, and are told that their own sons and daughters will be sold, through Judah, to Sheba.

Then the nations are summoned to war and told to hammer their plowshares into swords, and the LORD sits to judge: the harvest is ripe and the winepress is full. Crowds fill the valley of decision, sun and moon go dark, and the LORD roars from Zion and shakes heaven and earth, yet he is a refuge for his people. The book ends in a vision of Jerusalem holy, mountains dripping sweet wine, a spring flowing from the house of the LORD, Egypt and Edom waste, Judah lived in forever, and the LORD dwelling in Zion.
readings: Read as a future judgment of the nations

The valley is the place of the final judgment, when the nations that oppressed God's people are called to account and Zion is restored. This is how most Jewish and Christian interpreters have read it.
Read as a poetic reversal of the nations' crimes

Chapter 3 answers the grievances of chapter 1: the people who were sold are brought back, those who sold them are sold, the Temple that went without wine now has a spring flowing from it. The judgment is a mirror image of the injuries.
The valley, the harvest and the winepress are images that the New Testament picks up for the end of the age (Revelation 14:14-20), and need not be tied to one historical battle.

views.H: The crimes named (scattering, dividing the land, selling captives to the Greeks) point either to the Philistine and Arab raid in the reign of Jehoram of Judah (2 Chronicles 21:16-17), or to the sack of Jerusalem in 586 BC and the slave trade that followed; Greeks as buyers fit a late date most easily, and those who date the book early reply that Greek traders were already on the coast in the ninth or eighth century (the note at 3:6). Edom's and Egypt's violence against Judah (3:19) suits either the ninth century or the sixth. The valley of Jehoshaphat is a symbolic name for most commentators.
views.C: Chapter 3 (Hebrew 4) is often thought to be a later addition (Duhm), but most now take it as part of one book. The verse 'Pound your plowshares into swords' reverses Isaiah 2:4 and Micah 4:3, and 3:16 and 3:18 are word for word Amos 1:2 and nearly Amos 9:13, which is why Joel and Amos stand side by side in the Hebrew order of the Twelve. 3:21 is hard in Hebrew and in the old versions. Nogalski sees catchwords tying Joel to Amos and Obadiah.
views.J: Jewish tradition places the judgment of the nations at the end of days and links it with the war of Gog and Magog (Ezekiel 38-39) and with the coming of the Messiah. The valley of Jehoshaphat was identified with the Kidron Valley, east of Jerusalem, and Jews have long wished to be buried near it. Rashi reads the name Jehoshaphat as "the LORD's judgments", Ibn Ezra takes the valley as the Valley of Blessing (2 Chronicles 20:26), and Radak as named for the king or for the judgment (see the note at 3:2). The picture of Zion as the source of water and wine closes the book as a promise of the restored Jerusalem.
views.X: Christian writers have read 3:2, 12 and 14 as the Last Judgment, with the sickle and the winepress of 3:13 taken up in Revelation 14:14-20, and 3:18 as a picture of the water of life (Revelation 22:1). The valley of Jehoshaphat was identified with the Kidron Valley by the fourth century. This edition did not check the patristic commentaries on this chapter.
views.F: Dispensational teachers take 3:1-17 as the nations gathered at the end of the Great Tribulation, with the LORD's return to Zion and the judgment of the nations in Matthew 25:31-46, before the thousand years. Amillennial readers take the passage as the final judgment at Christ's return, in poetic form. Jewish messianic readings tie it to the war of Gog and Magog and the final redemption.

deep.b: Chapter 3 answers chapter 1 point by point. In chapter 1 the offering is cut off from the LORD's house; in 3:18 a spring flows out of it. In chapter 1 the wine is cut off from the drinkers' mouth; in 3:18 the mountains drip it. In chapter 1 the nation is attacked; in 3:9-12 the nations are summoned. In 3:3 children are sold for a drink; in 3:8 the sellers' children are sold. At the end the land that mourned is full of water, and the Temple that was empty has the LORD living in Zion. The book moves from locusts to a spring, and from the cutting off of the offerings to the water of the house of the LORD.

Isaiah 2:4 and Micah 4:3 picture an age when weapons are turned into farm tools. Joel 3:10 reverses the order: the farm tools become weapons. The context decides. In Isaiah the nations stream to Zion to be taught; in Joel they are summoned to judgment. Both come "in the last days" and both end at Zion, with the LORD as judge. Readers have used the reversal to say that Joel is a darker, more martial counterpart of Isaiah's peace, or that Joel shows the order of events: the great battle first and the peace after. The Plain keeps the wording exact, so that the reader hears Isaiah behind Joel.

echoes: Genesis 12:3; Isaiah 2:4; Isaiah 63:1-6; Ezekiel 38-39; Ezekiel 47:1-12; Obadiah 11, 15, 17; Amos 1:2; 9:13; Micah 4:3; Zechariah 14:2, 8; Matthew 25:31-32; Mark 4:29; Revelation 14:14-20; 16:16; 22:1

settings.what: The judgment of the nations and the case against Tyre, Sidon and Philistia
settings.to: Judah and Jerusalem, as the people the nations wronged; and, by name, Tyre, Sidon and the districts of Philistia
settings.when: 'In those days and at that time', when the LORD turns the fortunes of Judah and Jerusalem around
settings.why: To assure the survivors that their suffering is known and answered. The nations are summoned, charged and sentenced, and the sentence matches the crime: those who sold Judeans to the Greeks will have their own children sold. Knowing the first hearers shows that this is a comfort to the wronged, not a threat to be read by the nations.
settings.readers: For Judah in any age after a defeat, the passage said that the LORD would settle the account.
views: The raid of the Philistines and Arabs in Jehoram's day (2 Chronicles 21:16-17) and trade in captives by Tyre and Philistia.
The aftermath of 586 BC and the Phoenician and Greek slave trade of the Persian period.

settings.what: The summons to war, the harvest, and the roar from Zion
settings.by: The LORD and Joel (including a prayer in 3:11)
settings.to: The nations; and, behind them, the people of Judah, who hear that the LORD is their refuge
settings.when: At the day of the LORD, in the valley of decision
settings.why: To announce the end of the powers that have crushed God's people, and to give Zion's community a refuge. The nations are told to prepare for a war that will be a judgment. In the reader's mind the contrast is the final line: they will know that the LORD their God lives in Zion.
settings.readers: For the Twelve, the roar from Zion joins Joel to Amos 1:2; for Revelation it supplies the harvest and the winepress.
views: A last war of the nations against Jerusalem, as in Ezekiel 38-39 and Zechariah 14.
A court, with the LORD seated and the nations tried, not a fight.

settings.what: The blessing of Zion and the end of Egypt and Edom
settings.to: Judah and Jerusalem, the community that has fasted and been rescued
settings.why: To end the book on the shape of the promise: a land of wine, milk and water, a spring from the Temple, a people living there for good, and a God at home in Zion. Egypt and Edom are named as examples of the violent nations. The final line gives the book its answer to the question 'Where is their God?' (2:17): he lives in Zion.
settings.readers: For the Twelve, the mountains that drip wine close Joel as they close Amos (9:13).

traditions.q: Is the judgment of the nations in the Valley of Jehoshaphat a final judgment, a battle at Christ's return, or a symbol?
views: The Last Judgment follows the resurrection of all the dead, both the just and the unjust, and Christ will judge in glory (Catechism 1038-1039). The prophets' judgment of the nations is a figure of it, and Catholic teaching does not look for a thousand-year reign on earth.

The Last Judgment is the coming of Christ in glory to judge the living and the dead, shown in the icon of the Last Judgment; the judgment scenes of the prophets are read as images of that day, with the Church as the new Zion.
Christ will return visibly on the last day to judge the living and the dead (Augsburg Confession XVII); the Lutheran confessions reject an earthly thousand-year reign (Augsburg Confession XVII).

Amillennial and postmillennial Reformed teachers read Joel 3 as a poetic picture of the final judgment at Christ's return, which the Westminster Confession (chapter 33) describes as a single day on which all are judged.

Joel 3 is a prophecy of the judgment of the nations at Christ's second coming, at the end of the Great Tribulation, followed by the thousand-year kingdom with Israel restored in the land; Matthew 25:31-46 is the same event.
